---
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Fixed (singular) points and closed trajectories are called the \textit{critical elements}
of $X$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
A singular point $p$ of $X$ is \textit{hyperbolic} (non-degenerate) if the Jacobian matrix
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jacobian}
\left( \frac{\partial X_i}{\partial x_j}(p) \right)_{i,j=1}^{2},
\end{equation}
written in local coordinates, has no eigenvalue with zero real part. A closed trajectory
$\gamma$ is \textit{hyperbolic} if the differential at $p\in\gamma$ of the Poincar\'e return
map has no eigenvalue of absolute value $1$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
A point $y\in M$ is an $\omega$-limit ($\alpha$-limit) point of $x\in M$ if there is a
sequence $t_i\to+\infty$ ($t_i\to-\infty$) such that $\varphi_{t_i}(x)\to y$. The set of all
such points is the $\omega$-limit ($\alpha$-limit) set $\omega(x)$ ($\alpha(x)$).
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
The \textit{stable} and \textit{unstable manifolds} of a critical element $c$ are
\[
W^s(c)=\{x\in M \mid \omega(x)=c\},\qquad W^u(c)=\{x\in M \mid \alpha(x)=c\}.
\]
For a singular point $p$ this means $\lim_{t\to+\infty}\varphi_t(x)=p$ and
$\lim_{t\to-\infty}\varphi_t(x)=p$, respectively; in particular $p\in W^s(p)\cap W^u(p)$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
A point $p\in M$ is \textit{wandering} for $X$ if there are a neighborhood $V$ of $p$ and
$T>0$ such that $X_t(V)\cap V=\emptyset$ for all $|t|>T$; otherwise $p$ is
\textit{non-wandering}. The set of non-wandering points is denoted by $\Sigma(X)$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
A vector field $X$ on a compact surface $M$ is a \textit{Morse--Smale vector field} if
(1) $X$ has finitely many critical elements, all hyperbolic; (2) $\Sigma(X)$ is the union of
the critical elements; (3) the stable and unstable manifolds of critical elements intersect
transversally.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
A Morse--Smale flow is a \textit{Morse flow} if it has no closed trajectories. A Morse flow
on a closed surface $M$ is \textit{optimal} if it has the minimal number of singular points
among all Morse flows on $M$.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:optimal}
Let $M$ be a closed connected surface. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] a Morse flow on $M$ is optimal if and only if it has exactly one sink and exactly
  one source;
\item[(b)] an optimal Morse flow has $k=2-\chi(M)$ saddles; thus $k=2g$ if $M$ is orientable
  of genus $g$, and $k=h$ if $M$ is non-orientable of genus $h$.
\end{enumerate}
Optimal Morse flows exist on every closed connected surface.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $a$, $b$, $k$ be the numbers of sources, sinks and saddles of a Morse flow. The sum of
the indices of the singular points is $\chi(M)$ (Poincar\'e--Hopf), and a source or sink has
index $+1$, a saddle $-1$; hence $a+b-k=\chi(M)$ and the total number of singular points is
$a+b+k=2(a+b)-\chi(M)$. Since $\Sigma(X)$ is the finite set of singular points, $\omega(x)$ is
a single singular point $p$ for every $x$. Take $x$ outside the one-dimensional stable
manifolds of the saddles and outside the singular points; then $p$ is not a saddle, and not a
source (as $W^s(p)=\{p\}$ for a source), hence a sink. So $b\ge1$, and by time reversal $a\ge1$.
Therefore $a+b\ge2$ with equality exactly when $a=b=1$, which gives (a) and $k=2-\chi(M)$.
Existence is shown in \cite{Kybalko2018} (equivalently, via a Morse function with one
maximum and one minimum).
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:equiv}
Two vector fields $X,Y$ on $M$ are \textit{topologically (trajectory) equivalent},
$X\sim Y$, if there is a homeomorphism $h\colon M\to M$ that maps trajectories of $X$ onto
trajectories of $Y$ and preserves the direction of motion along them. The homeomorphism $h$
is not required to preserve an orientation of $M$.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
Let $h$ be a topological equivalence of $X$ and $Y$. Then $p$ is a singular point of $X$ iff
$h(p)$ is a singular point of $Y$; a trajectory of $X$ is closed iff its image is closed; and
$h$ maps the $\alpha$-limit ($\omega$-limit) set of every trajectory onto the $\alpha$-limit
($\omega$-limit) set of the image trajectory.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
A vector field $X\in\mathcal X^r(M)$, $r\ge1$, is \textit{structurally stable} if it has a
neighborhood $U(X)$ in the $C^r$-topology such that $Y\sim X$ for all $Y\in U(X)$.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
A \textit{chord diagram} $D$ with $k$ chords consists of a boundary circle $S^1$,
$2k$ distinct points on $S^1$, and $k$ chords connecting these points in pairs
(chords may cross when drawn in the disk).
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
A code $\mathbf{c}$ is in \textit{Restricted Growth String (RGS) canonical form} if
$c_0 = 1$, and for every $m$ with $1\le m<k$ the first occurrence of $m$ precedes the
first occurrence of $m+1$. For an arbitrary sequence $\mathbf{w}$ in which every label
occurs twice, its \textit{RGS normalization} relabels the chords in order of first
occurrence.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
A \textit{signed chord diagram} (or marked chord diagram) assigns a sign
$\sigma_i \in \{+1, -1\}$ to each chord $i \in \{1, \dots, k\}$.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
Two signed chord diagrams $D_1, D_2$ are \textit{isomorphic} if one can be transformed
into the other via a cyclic shift of the code and a relabeling of the chords (signs are
carried along with their chords). They are \textit{equivalent} if they can additionally
be related by a reversal (mirror reflection) of the boundary circle. We write
$D_1\simeq D_2$ for equivalence.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:one_cycle}
The signed chord diagram $D_X$ constructed above is a one-cycle diagram. Its chord cycle
is the boundary of the basin of attraction of the sink $y_0$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The set $\Gamma=\{x_0\}\cup\bigcup_{i}\overline{W^s(s_i)}$ is a bouquet of $k$ circles
embedded in $M$ (the loop number $i$ is formed by the two separatrices entering $s_i$).
Every point of $M\setminus\Gamma$ lies on a trajectory with $\omega$-limit $y_0$, so
$M\setminus\Gamma$ is the basin of attraction of the sink, which is an open disk.
Hence $\Gamma$ is a cellular embedding with a single face, and the boundary of this face,
read along $\partial U(x_0)$ and the chords, is exactly the traversal
\eqref{eq:step} with the signs defined above.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
A \textit{chord cycle} is the closed traversal path generated by \eqref{eq:step}. A
diagram is a \textit{one-cycle diagram} if $|Q|=2k$ and every label $1,\dots,k$ occurs
exactly twice in $\mathbf w$; equivalently, a single traversal covers all chords twice and
all $2k$ boundary arcs.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:dual}
If $D$ is a one-cycle diagram, then $D^*$ is a one-cycle diagram, $D^{**}\simeq D$,
$D$ and $D^*$ have the same (non-)orientable genus, and the class of $D^*$ depends only
on the class of $D$. Consequently, if $N$ is the number of equivalence classes,
$K$ the number of unordered pairs $\{[D],[D^*]\}$ and $s$ the number of self-dual
classes, then $s=2K-N$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
See \cite{Kybalko2018}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:dual_flow}
Two optimal Morse flows $X,Y$ are topologically equivalent if and only if $D_X\simeq D_Y$, and $X$ is topologically equivalent to the inverse flow $-Y$ if and only if $D_X\simeq D_Y^*$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
See \cite{Kybalko2018}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:dual_graph}
If a one-cycle signed chord diagram $D$ is interpreted as a cellular embedding of a
single-vertex graph (a bouquet of $k$ circles) on a closed surface $M$ with a single
2-cell, then the dual chord diagram $D^*$ specifies the cellular embedding of the
topological dual graph $G^*$ on $M$; $G^*$ is again a bouquet of $k$ circles with a
single 2-cell.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
